intro: I will ask eleven quick yes or no questions about how you feel, then take one blood-pressure reading, and tell you what to do next. This is decision support, not a diagnosis.
disclaimer: Illustrative triage logic for a demo. It is not a diagnosis and not a substitute for flight-surgeon-approved procedures.

headlines.red: Act now. Treat this as urgent.

red: Stop safety-critical work and sit or lie down somewhere safe.
Tell the crew medical officer now and start the emergency checklist.
Queue a priority message to the flight surgeon with these answers and readings.
amber: Rest, hydrate, and avoid heavy exercise until this settles.
Log how you feel and re-check in about 4 hours.
Tell the crew medical officer if it gets worse or does not settle.
green: No red flags from these answers and readings. Keep your normal routine.
Measure again at your next scheduled time, or sooner if something changes.

recheck.red: Do not wait for a re-check. Do the urgent steps first and re-measure only when the crew medical officer asks.
recheck.amber: Re-check blood pressure and pulse in 4 hours, or after 5 minutes of rest if a reading was raised.
recheck.green: Re-check at your next scheduled measurement, about 24 hours from now.

reading_prompt: Now take one blood-pressure reading with the cuff. Rest for 5 minutes, put the cuff on the upper arm at heart level and stay still. Enter the systolic, diastolic and pulse numbers, or press No cuff if you do not have one.
no_cuff: No cuff available, answering from symptoms only.

questions.text: Do you feel a sharp pain in your chest right now?
instructions: Stop what you are doing and sit down. Do not start or continue exercise.
If the pain is heavy or crushing, spreads to your arm, jaw or back, or comes with sweating, say so when you report, and get a 12-lead ECG if the kit has one.
Stay with another crew member until the crew medical officer has seen you.

followup.text: Is the pain worse when you take a deep breath, or when you press on your chest?
followup.yes: Pain that changes with breathing or pressing is often muscular, but it stays on the urgent list until it has been checked.
followup.no: Constant pain that does not change with breathing is treated as more concerning. Point this out when you report.

questions.text: Are you short of breath, or breathing faster than usual while sitting still?
instructions: Sit upright, loosen anything tight and breathe slowly and deeply.
Check the cabin air and CO2 alarms, and sit near a vent if the air feels stale.
If speaking a full sentence is hard, treat it as an emergency and call the crew medical officer.

questions.text: Do you feel faint, or have you fainted or nearly fainted today?
instructions: Sit or lie down now and raise your legs above heart level.
Do not stand up quickly, and ask a crewmate to stay with you.
If someone cannot be woken or is confused, start the emergency response.

questions.text: Has your vision changed suddenly, with blurring, loss of part of your view, or new flashes?
instructions: Stop tasks that need fine vision and rest your eyes.
Report it at once: a sudden change can be a sign of pressure or circulation problems.
Do not operate equipment until it has been checked.

questions.text: Do you have a severe or unusual headache right now?
instructions: Rest in a dim, quiet place and drink water.
Report it now, especially with a stiff neck, fever or vision change.
Note whether this is the worst headache you have had, and say so when you report.

questions.text: Is your heart racing, pounding or skipping beats while you are resting?
instructions: Sit down, breathe slowly and re-check your pulse after 5 minutes of rest.
Avoid exercise, caffeine and nicotine until it settles.
If it lasts more than 15 minutes, or you feel faint or breathless, treat it as urgent.

questions.text: Do you feel feverish, or have you had chills?
instructions: Take your temperature and re-check it in 4 hours.
Drink more fluids, rest, and limit close contact with the crew.
Start the infection checklist and notify the crew medical officer if it reaches 38 °C.

questions.text: Do you have a new cough, sore throat or congested nose?
instructions: Wear a mask near crewmates and wipe shared surfaces.
Keep fluids up and sleep a full 8 hours.
Report it if breathing becomes hard or the cough deepens.

questions.text: Do you feel dizzy or lightheaded, especially when you sit up or stand?
instructions: Sit or lie down and rise slowly for the next few hours.
Drink 500 ml of water if you can tolerate it, and eat something salty.
If you faint or your vision greys out, treat it as urgent.

questions.text: Is there new swelling in your legs, ankles or face?
questions.finding: New swelling in the legs or face
instructions: Note where the swelling is and whether it pits when pressed.
Reduce salt, keep moving gently, and do not sit still for long periods.
Report it, especially with breathlessness or a rapid change in weight.

questions.text: Have you felt low, anxious or unlike yourself today?
instructions: Tell a crewmate you trust how you are feeling.
Protect an 8-hour sleep window and plan one restorative activity today.
Ask the ground flight psychologist for a private conference if this lasts more than a few days.
Lie down and raise your legs above heart level. Do not stand until you feel steady.
Drink 500 ml of water and ask a crewmate to stay with you.
Notify the crew medical officer and queue a priority message with these readings.
notes: Low blood pressure together with dizziness can mean dehydration or a circulation problem, so this is treated as urgent.

combinations.finding: Severe headache with high blood pressure
instructions: Sit quietly and re-check the cuff on the other arm after 5 minutes.
If it is still high, or you have vision change, chest pain or weakness, treat it as an emergency.
Notify the crew medical officer now. Do not take anything to lower it without advice.
notes: A severe headache with very high blood pressure needs a person, not just a re-check.

instructions: Sit or lie down, breathe slowly for 5 minutes and re-check the pulse.
If it stays above 120 at rest, or you feel faint or breathless, treat it as an emergency.
Notify the crew medical officer and queue a priority message.
notes: A racing heart that stays fast at rest is treated as urgent rather than watched.
